NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (
FSSAI
) has launched a nationwide surveillance exercise to assess the quality of packaged drinking water, with the results expected to take at least one to two months, FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani said.
The exercise is being carried out across the country as part of the food safety regulator's ongoing efforts to examine various food categories and ensure compliance with prescribed standards.
"That process has started, and we're doing it across the country. The results will take at least a month or two," Punhani told reporters.
He clarified that packaged drinking water was not selected for any specific reason but was part of the regulator's broader surveillance programme.
"Last year, we took up dairy, meat, eggs, cereals, energy drinks, sugary drinks and other products. So, water is also part of the process," he added.
Separately, Punhani stressed the need for food businesses to follow ethical advertising practices, particularly when making claims about their products and promoting them.
He emphasised that the regulator was not looking at the issue solely from a legal perspective and urged industry players to consider the ethical dimensions of advertising.
"The idea is not that it's only the legal part of it. It is also the ethical part of it," he said, calling on the industry to focus on responsible advertising practices.
The Bisleri row
Punhani's remarks and the nationwide surveillance exercise come amid regulatory action against packaged drinking water manufacturer Bisleri International over a sample collected from its Goa facility.
On November 23, the FSSAI granted sanction to prosecute the company after a regulatory sample was initially found non-compliant with the prescribed limits for bromate and declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Following an appeal by the company, the sample was sent to a referral food laboratory for further examination, which also declared it unsafe after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
However, the FSSAI clarified on Monday that the action was limited to a single sample from one batch, numbered GO 270, collected from the company's plant at Verna Electronic City in South Goa.

FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) said the food regulator is collecting samples of packaged drinking water from across the country and lab testing will be complete in around two months.
He also announced that FSSAI would soon start inspection of 'packaging materials' used for food items, saying those should be 'food grade'.
Bisleri responds to FSSAI findings, says bromate within permissible limits in Goa batch
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has widened the scope of its scrutiny after a sample of Bisleri packaged drinking water failed the lab test.
The regulator has
sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International.
When asked about its enforcement drive against packaged drinking water, Mr. Punhani said, "We are in the process. The process has started. We are doing all over the country."
On the timeline for results, he said, "It's a very big country. So I think it will take at least a month or two."
The CEO said the drive on packaged drinking water is not for any particular reason but part of the FSSAI efforts to safeguard consumers' interest by ensuring safe food.
Why has the FSSAI sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri? | Explained
"There is no particular reason. If you notice, in the last year, we have taken up, one by one, a lot of things. We have done dairy, meat, eggs, cereals, energy drinks, and sugary drinks. Water is also part of that process," he told reporters on the sidelines of a CII event.
Mr. Punhani highlighted that FSSAI has taken action against misleading advertisements as well as claims on the labelling of food products.
Asked about when the regulator will start the legal process against Bisleri International, Mr. Punhani said it is a "normal routine thing and it will happen".
Earlier, sources had said that FSSAI officials have carried out inspections of the premises of all major food business operators (FBOs) engaged in packaged water business and took samples for lab testing.
FSSAI would take legal action against companies if their samples fail the lab test and they are found to be violating the rules and regulations, sources had said.
Prosecution against Bisleri
On Sunday, through a social media post, FSSAI informed that it has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd regarding "unsafe packaged drinking water".
A regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" was collected from the premises of Bisleri International for analysis.
"The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006," the regulator had said.
Upon appeal by the company, the sample was sent to the referral food laboratory, which also declared it "unsafe" due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the regulator added.
The findings of the lab established violations relating to unsafe food under the law.
On Monday, Bisleri International asserted that its packaged drinking water is "safe" for consumption, and it will cooperate with the food regulator to address the issue.

news_title: CM Suvendu Adhikari directs cinema halls to allot prime-time slot to Bengali film on Hindu saint

efet_body:
CM Suvendu Adhikari directs cinema halls to allot prime-time slot to Bengali film on Hindu saint
The decision came days after a section of cinema hall owners in Bengal announced that the screening of the Bengali movie would be discontinued from November 27.
Published on: Nov 25, 2026, 15:47:59 IST
By
HT Correspondent
Share via

West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Tuesday directed cinema hall owners in the state to allot prime-time slots to “Sadhak Bamakhyapa”, a newly released Bengali movie on the spiritual journey of the 19th-century Tantric saint and mystic.
West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari met the film exhibitors and film distributors in the state. (PTI File)
more
The decision came days after a section of cinema hall owners in the state announced that the screening of the Bengali movie would be discontinued from November 27 to make way for the Ayushmann Khurrana-starrer Yeh Prem Mol Liya. The Bollywood movie is set to release in theatres on Friday.
“We are very happy. The chief minister has directed cinema hall owners to screen the movie. No exhibitors can deny space to the movie,” Sayantan Ghosal, director of the Bengali movie, told the media.
In an earlier statement, the makers of “Sadhak Bamakhyapa” had called the discontinuation of the movie's theatrical run “disheartening”.
“The decision to discontinue the theatrical run of Sadhak Bamakhyapa from this Friday is an extremely disheartening one for us, especially when the film has been receiving such overwhelming love and appreciation from audiences,” said an earlier statement by the film’s makers.
It also said that since the film’s release on November 20, it has received an encouraging response, with audiences turning out in significant numbers and several shows recording houseful occupancy, even on weekdays.
“However, with the upcoming release of Yeh Prem Mol Liya, produced by Rajshri Productions and distributed by YRF, we have been informed by exhibitors about the challenges of accommodating adequate shows for Sadhak Bamakhyapa from this Friday,” it had said.
CM's intervention
On Tuesday, Adhikari met the film exhibitors and film distributors in the state. The issue came up during the meeting.
“It is not just a question of screening the movie Sadhak Bamakhyapa. He directed cinema hall owners to screen at least one Bengali movie during the prime time. He also warned that the license of the cinema halls would be cancelled if Bengali movies are not allotted space,” Rudranil Ghosh, actor and BJP MLA, told the media after the meeting.
“Bengali cinema got a new life after today’s meeting because of chief minister Suvendu Adhikari,” an SVF spokesperson said.

BENGALURU: The Supreme Court on Wednesday cancelled the bail granted to former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni in the 2016 murder of BJP worker and Dharwad zilla panchayat member Yogeshgouda Goudar, setting aside the Karnataka High Court’s July 31, 2026 order that suspended his life sentence and stayed his conviction.
The apex court’s decision withdraws the relief granted by the high court while Kulkarni’s criminal appeal was pending. The high court had ordered his release on bail after suspending the life sentence imposed by a special court for elected representatives.
Kulkarni and 16 others were convicted of murder and criminal conspiracy in the case. The special court sentenced all 17 to life imprisonment after finding them guilty of plotting and executing Goudar’s killing.
Goudar, a BJP zilla panchayat member, was hacked to death at a gym in Saptapur, Dharwad, on June 15, 2016. The local police initially investigated the case, which was transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation in 2019 after allegations of political pressure and claims that Kulkarni, then a district in-charge minister, had orchestrated the killing.
The CBI arrested Kulkarni on Nov 5, 2020, naming him the main conspirator.
The Supreme Court granted him conditional bail on Aug 11, 2021, with a restriction on entering Dharwad district. It cancelled that bail on June 7, 2025, after allegations of attempts to influence or tamper with witnesses.
The apex court granted Kulkarni bail again on Feb 27, 2026, after key witnesses had been examined and directed that the trial be concluded expeditiously. He was convicted along with the other accused on April 15, 2026, and all 17 were sentenced to life imprisonment on April 17.

In the distance, urban buildings and residential layouts extend toward the horizon under a soft, slightly hazy sky. TOI Photo: Delhi News
New Delhi:
Nearly nine out of 10 women, girls and LGBTQ+ persons surveyed in Delhi do not feel safe in their neighbourhood parks after dark, while an overwhelming majority feel unsafe walking to the nearest bus stop or metro station at night, a study by the Centre for Equity and Inclusion (CEQUIN) has found.
Titled ‘Everyday Journeys: Women’s and Girls’ Access to Footpaths and Public Parks in Delhi’, the study highlights how poor infrastructure, harassment and a lack of institutional accountability continue to restrict women’s access to public spaces.
The survey received 1,882 responses, of which 1,588 were considered valid. It covered women, girls and LGBTQ+ persons and was conducted between Oct 15 and Nov 2, 2026.
The findings were supplemented by two focus group discussions, one involving nine college students and another with 11 women from neighbourhoods that included Jamia Nagar, Seelampur, Seemapuri and Tehkhand.
According to the report, 88.9% of respondents do not feel safe in the nearest public park after dark.
This figure remains high even during daytime, when 54% said they feel unsafe in parks.
Among the 1,114 respondents who answered a question on commuting, 87.5% said they did not feel safe walking to the nearest bus stop or metro station after dark.
The study identified both infrastructure gaps and men’s behaviour as major contributors to this fear. While 76.4% reported poorly lit footpaths, 60% said the footpaths leading to public transport points were either broken or missing.
As many as 79.5% said men’s behaviour — staring, making comments, whistling and following them — made their daily commutes unsafe.
A significant finding was the lack of awareness about civic accountability.
While 52.3% did not know where to complain about problems with footpaths or parks, 80.5% could not identify even one authority responsible for maintaining them.
The report also flagged the absence of women in public parks as a factor reinforcing the insecurity. As many as 42.7% of respondents who said they saw hardly any women in their parks in the evening also felt unsafe there after dark.
“Safety is not only about headline crimes. It is shaped by the everyday breakdown of lighting, footpaths, neighbourhood parks and institutional accountability,” Lora K.
Prabhu, co-founder and managing director of CEQUIN, said.
The organisation is set to submit the study and its recommendations to the Supreme Court in the ongoing suo motu cognisance taken on Sept 28following rape incidents in Delhi-NCR.
The submission seeks the court’s consideration of four priority measures -- better-lit and repaired footpaths, clear accountability for civic agencies, more women police personnel on evening patrols, and binding minimum safety standards for public parks.
CEQUIN will release the report Wednesday, marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and Girls, at its annual Hain Haq Hamara Hissedari event in Vasant Vihar.

The
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
(FSSAI) said on November 22 that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd over a packaged drinking water sample declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
A sanction lets the regulator take a case to court. It is not a finding of guilt, and Bisleri says its water is safe. The case has revived questions India has asked of packaged water for two decades: what is tested, how often, and what happens when results are disputed.
FSSAI drew six samples from Bisleri’s Goa facility on September 30, 2025. Five passed. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre (µg/L), against a prescribed limit of 10. The sample fell in the category “packaged drinking water (other than mineral water)”, which covers water from any potable source, including public supply systems.
Bisleri appealed in November 2025, and a referral food laboratory retested the sample. It found bromate within the limit but detected polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). FSSAI declared the sample unsafe on that basis. FSSAI’s standard does not permit PAHs at detectable levels. The regulator has not published the concentration or the compounds found. No recall has been ordered.
Bisleri says the matter concerns a single batch made in Goa in September 2025. It says retests by approved laboratories showed bromate within the limit, and that it sent the independent results to FSSAI’s Western Regional Office in a letter dated February 2, 2026.
The company says it received no notice by email or hard copy, and believed the matter was resolved. It says it runs more than 90 tests across a 10-step manufacturing process, that the Goa unit is one of 143 plants, and that it will keep cooperating with the regulator.
Earlier cases
Packaged water has faced scrutiny before. In
February 2003
, the Centre for Science and Environment reported pesticide residues after testing 34 bottles of 17 brands sold in the Delhi region, including the top sellers Bisleri, Bailley, Pure Life, Aquafina, and Kinley. On average, samples held 36.4 times more pesticide than the European limit the group used as its yardstick. The government appointed an inquiry committee the next day and accepted its recommendations on the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).
In 2015, scientists at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre tested 18 brands of packaged water in Mumbai. About 27 per cent of samples exceeded 10 µg/L of bromate, and readings reached 43.
Government data show a continuing pattern. Parliament was told in January 2019 that 496 of 1,123 samples analysed in 2017-18 did not conform to standards. In April 2025, Karnataka’s Health Minister Dinesh Gundu Rao said that of 255 samples analysed in a State survey, 95 were unsafe and 88 substandard. Most problem samples came from local manufacturers, he said, and national brands generally kept higher standards.
In May, a consumer complaint on FSSAI’s Food Safety Connect portal led to an inspection of an alkaline water plant at Savli, Vadodara. FSSAI seized stock worth about Rs.31.61 lakh over misbranding, visible particles, and an unpermitted substance.
Global scrutiny
The pressure is not Indian alone. In 2024, Nestlé Waters admitted to using banned filters and ultraviolet treatment on mineral waters in France, and paid a €2 million fine to avoid legal action. A French Senate inquiry said in May 2025 that the government had covered up the practice. Nestlé says the filters it now uses are permitted, and its water is pure. The case turned on treatment that French and European rules prohibit for natural mineral water.
A January 2024 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found about 240,000 plastic fragments in an average litre of bottled water across three US brands, about 90 per cent of them nanoplastics. The researchers said much of the plastic seemed to come from the bottle and the reverse osmosis filter. A co-author said it is not known whether the particles are dangerous. The International Bottled Water Association said such reports “unnecessarily scare consumers.”
A 2023 United Nations University report put global bottled water sales at about $270 billion and 350 billion litres in 2021. It warned that the industry’s unrestricted growth can slow progress towards safe water for all.

Interestingly, a LocalCircles survey found, as per multiple news reports, that just 1 per cent of respondents said they rely on bottled water for drinking and cooking instead of treating municipal water, highlighting the limited reliance on packaged water as a primary source for household consumption.
84% use purifiers or RO systems
The survey, covering 29,161 responses from urban households across 284 districts, found that 40 per cent use water purifiers, while 44 per cent rely on RO systems. Another 9 per cent said they boil water before consuming it, while 1 per cent use chlorination, alum or other mineral-based methods. A further 1 per cent reported using other methods to treat water.
Trust in tap water declines
Only 2 per cent of respondents said they consume piped water directly without purification. The proportion of households confident about the safety of untreated municipal water has also declined sharply, from 6 per cent in the 2025 survey to 2 per cent in the latest exercise.
The findings come at a time when packaged drinking water brands are facing increased scrutiny following FSSAI's enforcement action against Bisleri International.
FSSAI sanctions prosecution against Bisleri

testing found a bromate level
of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
Bisleri says issue limited to one batch
Bisleri, however, maintained that its packaged drinking water is safe for consumption
and said the issue was restricted to a single batch manufactured at its Goa facility in September 2025. The company said five of the six samples collected from the plant on September 30, 2025, met the applicable standards, while one sample was found to have a marginally higher bromate level.
The company has said it will cooperate with food safety authorities as FSSAI expands its enforcement drive across major packaged drinking water brands.

“Bisleri produces more than 50,000 batches annually. FSSAI’s sale prohibition applies only to one batch, GO 270, manufactured in Goa on 27 September 2025. There are no stocks of this batch in the market currently,” the Chauhan family-promoted firm said in a statement.

The specific compounds detected and their concentrations are important in determining the potential health implications of any contamination.

Bromate is a compound that can form during some water-disinfection processes. PAHs are a group of chemical compounds; FSSAI said a referral laboratory detected them in the sample.

After the company appealed, the sample was sent to the referral food laboratory, which also declared it unsafe because of the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. The lab findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the law, and FSSAI granted sanction to launch prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd.
Bisleri says its water is safe and it will cooperate
On Monday, Bisleri International said its packaged drinking water is safe for consumption and that it will cooperate with the food regulator to address the issue. The company said it has not received any notice by email or in hard copy so far, and it has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI's website. Bisleri also said drinking water safety is a priority and that it maintains stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across its 10-step manufacturing process.
What remains unclear after the regulator's announcement
The action against Bisleri International is part of the ongoing enforcement drive, and a source said the prosecution sanction is part of this exercise being undertaken in the public interest. The regulator did not name the other packaged drinking water brands sampled, and it did not say how many samples were collected or how many premises were inspected.

Bisleri drinking water safe or not: FSSAI finds bromate level 20% above limit; what are the possible cancer risks? here's what consumers need to know.
FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a packaged drinking water sample collected from its Goa facility was declared unsafe following laboratory tests for bromate and polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). The action paves the way for legal proceedings against the company over alleged violations of food safety standards.
Bisleri has disputed the findings, saying subsequent independent tests found bromate levels within the prescribed limit. The case has brought attention to bromate, a chemical that can form during drinking water disinfection and is regulated because of concerns about the health effects of prolonged exposure.
What happened to the Bisleri water sample?
According to Bisleri, FSSAI collected six samples from its Goa facility on September 30, 2025. Five met the applicable standards, while one recorded bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
The company appealed against the initial finding on November 22, 2025. A referral laboratory subsequently declared the sample unsafe after detecting PAHs, FSSAI said.
Bisleri said it also arranged independent testing at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which found bromate within the permissible limit. It submitted the results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office in a letter dated February 2, 2026.
Live Events
The company said it received no further communication and believed the matter had been closed. It also claimed it had not received a notice by email or in hard copy.
FSSAI has nevertheless sanctioned prosecution against the company. This permits legal proceedings to be initiated but does not amount to a conviction.
Bisleri said drinking water safety was a priority and that it conducted more than 90 quality tests across its 10-step manufacturing process. It also said it would cooperate with the regulator. These are the company's claims, while the prosecution action follows FSSAI's laboratory findings.
What is bromate and how does it enter drinking water?
Bromate is a chemical compound that can form during water treatment. One of its main sources in drinking water is ozonation, a disinfection process in which ozone is used to destroy microorganisms.
When ozone reacts with naturally occurring bromide ions in source water, bromate can form as a by-product. The amount produced depends on factors such as bromide concentration, ozone dosage, pH and water quality.
Bromate can also form in certain hypochlorite solutions used for disinfection. Its presence does not necessarily mean that the chemical was deliberately added to the water. It can develop during treatment, which is why manufacturers must control the process and test the finished product.
What is the safe limit for bromate in drinking water?
World Health Organization (WHO) has set a provisional guideline value of 0.01 milligrams per litre, equivalent to 10 micrograms per litre.
The 12 micrograms per litre recorded in the initial Bisleri sample was therefore 2 micrograms above the prescribed limit, or 20% higher.
The limit is designed to control exposure over time.
What can bromate do to the human body?
The principal health concern associated with bromate is cancer risk following prolonged exposure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified potassium bromate as possibly carcinogenic to humans, based on evidence from animal studies.
WHO's assessment refers to animal experiments in which long-term exposure to bromate was associated with tumours, including in the kidneys and thyroid. Laboratory research has also found evidence of genetic damage.
However, evidence of cancer-causing effects in humans is inadequate. The classification does not mean that everyone exposed to bromate will develop cancer.
Exposure to very high amounts can also cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Kidney and nervous system effects, as well as hearing loss, have been reported in cases involving high exposure. These effects should not be confused with the health implications of the concentration reported in the Bisleri sample.
What does the Bisleri case mean for consumers?
The dispute concerns a regulatory sample collected from Bisleri's Goa facility. Bisleri has challenged the findings and cited subsequent tests that it says found bromate within the permitted limit.
The case comes amid tighter scrutiny of packaged drinking water manufacturers. FSSAI removed the mandatory Bureau of Indian Standards certification requirement for packaged drinking water and mineral water in October 2024. It introduced a mandatory testing scheme from January 1, 2026, requiring manufacturers to conduct prescribed tests, maintain batch-wise records and take corrective action when samples fail safety requirements.

Before entering Bollywood with Farah Khan’s 'Om Shanti Om' in 2007, Deepika Padukone underwent a three-month acting course at Anupam Kher’s Mumbai-based institute, Actor Prepares. She made her debut opposite

She was a well-known model. Farah decided to cast her in the film with Shah Rukh Khan. It was a 3-month course. Because Deepika was a model and came from a very educated background, she was very prim and proper. She would do everything properly. She used to pick up the cup of tea with that style. Sometimes, there was no believability.”
The maid exercise that challenged Deepika Padukone
Anupam then described an exercise that required Deepika to portray a domestic worker sweeping the floor.
However, he felt that she continued performing the task with the same charm and elegance. To help her understand the difference, he invited his domestic helper to demonstrate the action in front of the students. The demonstration showed him the natural approach he wanted Deepika to recreate.
“One day, I was taking the class and told her to play a maid, who has to just sweep the floor. She was doing that also with a charm.
Then, I called my home maid and asked her to sweep the floor. She did it with total conviction,” he said.

Bisleri says it will cooperate after FSSAI sanctions prosecution
NEW DELHI: Packaged drinking water major Bisleri International Pvt Ltd on Monday maintained that its products remain safe for consumption, after the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (
FSSAI
) sanctioned prosecution against the company over a sample of its packaged drinking water declared unsafe.
“Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across our 10-step manufacturing process and will continue to cooperate with FSSAI to address the matter through the appropriate regulatory process. A trusted brand for years, Bisleri remains safe for consumption,” the company said.
In a detailed media statement, Bisleri said the regulatory matter concerned a single batch manufactured in September 2025 at its Goa facility, one of 143 plants in its network.
The company also said it had not received any official notice from the food regulator.
“We are aware of recent media reports that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued a notice to Bisleri. The matter dates back approximately 14 months, to a batch produced in September 2025 at Bisleri’s Goa manufacturing facility, one of 143 plants in our network,” the statement said.
Bisleri disputes laboratory findings
According to the company, the FSSAI collected six samples from its Goa facility on September 30, 2025.
Initial tests found that five samples met all applicable standards, while the sixth recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
Following an appeal by Bisleri on November 22, 2025, the sample was sent to a referral laboratory for further testing. The laboratory found the bromate level to be within the prescribed limit but separately detected polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
Bisleri said the difference between the test results raised questions that required clarification. It subsequently arranged for the same sample to be tested independently at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which also found the bromate level to be within the prescribed limit.
The company said it submitted the independent test results to the FSSAI's Western Regional Office along with a formal letter dated February 2, 2026.
“We submitted the independent test results to FSSAI’s Western Regional Office with a formal letter dated 2 February 2026. We received no further communication from FSSAI after that submission and understood the matter to be closed. To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI’s website,” the company said.

The company's statement followed the FSSAI's announcement that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri over the packaged drinking water sample.
In a social media post, the regulator said a sample of “Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)” collected from the company's premises did not comply with prescribed bromate limits and was declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
After Bisleri appealed against the findings, the sample was sent to a referral food laboratory, which also declared it unsafe after detecting PAHs, the FSSAI said.
The regulator said the findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the law, leading it to sanction prosecution against the company.
Four other food businesses face prosecution
The FSSAI has also sanctioned prosecution against four other food businesses: Vasant Masala Pvt Ltd, Tit-Bit Foods India Pvt Ltd, Mimansa Industries and Asha Confectionery.

The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
“Upon appeal by the food business operator (FBO), the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory, which also declared it unsafe due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs),” FSSAI said. When they exceed safe limits, several PAHs can be toxic.

India's packaged-food sector is under sharper regulatory scrutiny after the

, ordering a halt to bhujia production at one of its facilities. The action, triggered by an inspection that flagged multiple compliance failures, underscores how hygiene, labelling and licensing lapses can quickly escalate into enforcement action in a category where consumer trust is critical.
The immediate concern for the regulator was not just the quality of a single batch, but the broader manufacturing process. Inspectors found practices that raised questions about food handling standards, the status of production permissions and the integrity of stock already in the system. In a business built on scale and shelf life, such findings can have wider implications for distribution, retailer confidence and brand reputation.
Inspection findings prompted a production stop
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has directed
CG Foods
India to stop manufacturing veg bhujia after an inspection allegedly uncovered serious violations at the unit. The order came after officials identified lapses that included the re-processing of noodles collected from the floor without proper heat treatment, according to the inspection findings.
Such a practice, if established, would point to a breakdown in basic hygiene controls and internal quality systems. In food manufacturing, especially in snack categories that move through long distribution chains, contamination risks and process deviations are treated as high-priority compliance issues because they can affect both consumer safety and product consistency.
Licensing and packaging issues added to the case
Beyond the hygiene concerns, the inspection also reportedly found that some manufacturing activity was being carried out without the necessary licence. Officials further flagged predated packaging, a violation that can mislead buyers and complicate traceability when products are recalled or audited.
These are not minor procedural errors. For a packaged-food business, licensing gaps can raise questions about whether a plant is authorised for the exact product being made, while incorrect packaging dates can undermine confidence in expiry management and inventory rotation. Together, the findings suggest the regulator viewed the matter as a systemic compliance failure rather than an isolated lapse.
More than 32,000 kg of stock seized
As part of the enforcement action, the regulator seized more than 32,000 kg of stock, indicating the scale of the inventory that came under scrutiny. The seizure signals that the inspection was not limited to observation and documentation, but moved into direct control of product that may no longer be considered fit for market circulation until the matter is resolved.
Legal proceedings have also been initiated, adding a formal enforcement layer to the case. In regulatory disputes of this kind, the legal track often determines whether penalties, further restrictions or corrective measures follow, depending on what is established during the process.
Why the case matters for the packaged-snacks market
The action against CG Foods comes at a time when India’s food regulator has been pushing for tighter compliance across packaged foods, where scale often leaves little room for operational shortcuts. Snack makers, in particular, depend on consistent production hygiene, accurate labelling and clean audits because their products are widely distributed and frequently consumed without further processing.
The episode also highlights the reputational risk attached to manufacturing lapses in an industry where brands compete on convenience as much as on trust. A plant-level violation can quickly become a brand-wide issue if retailers, distributors and consumers begin to question the controls behind the product.
For CG Foods, the immediate challenge will be to address the regulator's findings and restore confidence in its manufacturing systems. For the wider sector, the case serves as a reminder that food safety compliance is not just a legal obligation but a commercial one, especially in categories where products travel far from the factory before reaching the consumer.
